text_fidelity_a:
THINKWARE F550 Full HD Dash Cam with high-speed Cortex A8 Processor, GPS Tracker & Dual Save Technology I've tried some low-cost in-car cams and have been unimpressed with the build quality or video quality of the devices. The Thinkware 550 was a marked departure - it feels very well-built and solid. I'd rate the build quality up there with a decent conventional camcorder, such as a Sony. It also looks very attractive - they did a great job with the design.

This is not an "action cam" type of device for uploading videos of during stupid stuff onto Youtube (sorry, showing my age here - I probably would have done the same had cams been around in my youth). Rather, it's a cam for automatically documenting events that occur while driving (such as a crash or other incident) without any need for user action. Video files are time and date stamped, and assigned a location using GPS. It's more of a "black box" type recording device for a car rather than a "fun time" action cam with a car mount.

You can also use this while parked and with a rear camera, but both of those require additional items not included with this package (hard wire install for parking use; a separate camera for rear view use).

Installation is easy but also a little bit tricky. The mount is a plastic cradle with an adhesive backing. Once you determine where you want the cam mounted (up on the windshield is the recommended position) you peel off the backing on the adhesive pad and stick it to the windshield. It's a permanent mount (well, you can remove it from the glass, but it can't be reused). Easy to do, but tricky in that you really need to take some time before committing to a location and think through where the power cord needs to be routed.

The unit is lightweight (5.1 ounces without the cradle) and seems to be holding well to the windshield even over very bumpy terrain.. The manual suggests leaving the cam off the cradle until the adhesive has cured for 24 hours. I didn't see that tip until after I tested its holding ability over broken road. So if you miss that tip as well, it doesn't seem to be a problem.

The cam does not have a built-in battery. It must be powered by an included cigarette lighter adapter (known by "power ports" these days, but I still call them cigarette lighters). The adapter is very nicely made with a stout cord. That's good for longevity; not so good for routing it so the cord is not visible or in the way. There are some adhesive tabs included to lasso down the cable to help make for a neat (or semi-neat) install. I'll probably add some electrical tape to neaten up the install a bit more.

The manufacturer also cautions to make sure the power port you use gets shut off when you turn off the engine. The cam can continue to pull power if the power port is live, potentially draining your car's battery.

It automatically powers up when you start the car. It can be manually turned off (or back on) as well. It offers two recording modes: continuous (which is in one minute segments) or on-demand (you can manually start and stop). It also states that when there is an impact, the cam will store the 10 seconds before and the 10 seconds after in a secure memory folder. I'll have to take their word for that - can't really test that out! Under normal circumstances, when the micro SD card fills up it starts overwriting old files.

A micro SD card is included along with a reader. The card holds the user manual and the software, so it can't really be used to store video files. I used my own card reader rather than the one included since the included one was too tiny for my clumsy fingers to deal with.

There is no viewer on the cam - you have to take out the SD card and pull up the files using the included software. That for me is the biggest problem and limitation of this device. You have to trust that it's working since there's no confirmation other than the indicator lights and prompts. Nor can you set the camera specs unless you have access to a PC.

On the plus side, the lack of a screen means there's no risk of driver distraction while the cam is operating. I can't fault that. Still, I would have liked to see a design that has a screen that remains off until the camera is out of the mount so it can be used in-car to change settings or review stored video. That maintains the lack of driver distraction but still allows for better use of the cam while parked.

What makes up for a lot of these shortfalls is the video quality. Great - really great. Crisp, clear and sharp. It provides a panoramic view (the specs say 140 degrees) that easily covers the full view from the windshield. You really won't believe this is from a car cam. It dealt with head-on full sunlight pretty well, and did a decent job at night. I did get a fair amount of reflection off the windshield at night, but the video was very workable.

The included software installed fine on a Win 7 machine after I suspended Avast from running - this software does not want to work and play well with Avast. I even had to keep Avast suspended while running the software. Not tough to use - got the hang of it from just trying out menu options and playing around. It will ask to install an update right off the bat.

The video quality and overall "forget about it and it just records" type of operation are strong pluses. The power cord, mounting system, and lack of a view screen are problems. Weighing everything together gets me to a 3.5 star rating which I'll round up to 4 stars since the video quality is so nice. If you can live with the limitations, this is well worth considering.
text_fidelity_b: THINKWARE F550 Full HD Dash Cam with high-speed Cortex A8 Processor, GPS Tracker & Dual Save Technology

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin nüvi 360 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Text-To-Speech (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I've had this Nuvi 360 since Dec, 2006. It really works well. I carried it with me to DC. Even on foot it was terrific. It knew where all the restaurants and points of interest were and faithfully navigated us around the ancient horse paths of the Virginia/DC area. Believe me, when you pop out of an underground Metro station in the middle of the night and have no idea where you are or which direction to head off in, the ol' Garmin was there.

It's so small it easily fits in a pocket. The built-in battery lasts reasonably long. In the car, the 12-Volt adapter allows the unit to stay on indefinitely. You can select which accent and which gender you want the voice prompts to speak. Australian "Bruce," American "Jill" and a host of other combinations. All very fun. The voice prompts are the best. You really don't need to look at the thing while driving because it's uncanny in telling you what to do when you need to do it. It is amazingly accurate: something like 20 feet. It takes you right to the destination driveway.

It acquires the sats quickly and doesn't get flustered if you violate its recommendation and go in a different route. It just says, "recalculating" and finds another route for you. None of this "make a U-turn, bonehead!" It gives you enough time to make the turns, too. Also, it displays how far it is until the next turn. Very nice. No need to worry if you've missed it.

If you are planning on going to Europe, buy the unit that comes preloaded with both US and Europe maps as purchasing the Europe maps after the fact will really jump the cost unnecessarily.

I haven't used the Bluetooth capability yet but might later...after I get a Bluetooth phone.

The display is quite viewable in daylight and very bright at night, though it can be set to auto-dim at sundown so it's not too bright at night. You can touch the screen and scroll the map under your finger much like Google Maps can, to preview your route if desired. It shows coordinates and you can save them as destinations if desired, even if the location doesn't have an official street address. It is an MP3 player and can display photos and play Audible books on tape. When you are using the MP3 or Audible features, it pauses the file playing back to announce directions, then returns to the file without losing any of the MP3 file or book info. Very nice.

At extra cost, it has the ability to add foreign language dictionaries which can verbally speak phrases and words to you. You can also add Travel Guides and other software via the SD chip slot.

Overall, I'm very pleased with this device. It's accurate, fast, functional and small.

The one thing that doesn't work is the windshield suction mount. It broke before I even used it once. The plastic loops on the suction cup that receive the ball arm's hinge pin are too thin and fragile and broke with just a little normal hinge adjustment.

I recommend the model 010-10908-00 friction mount that looks like a bean bag with a ball arm sticking up. I made something similar by taking an unneeded 1/4" thick mousepad and epoxying a couple of small 1" x 1" angle brackets to the pad to hold the ball arm that I salvaged from the broken suction cup mount.

A friction mount is interchangeable with multiple vehicles, doesn't slide around on the dash and allows complete and rapid removal and/or hiding to avoid theft. Plus, you don't have to glue a disk to the dash for the suction cup to attach to.

UPDATE 10-22-07:
The 360 works well enough; better than most. It should: Five point three bills should deliver one heck of a map!

I've had it since Dec 2006...less than one year. Today I get an offer from Garmin to update my North American map software for a mere point seven bills. That's AFTER the five point three bills I already sunk into this little electronic gizmo.

I heard Garmin has a one year free map update policy, but their website won't let me do it. Not cool. The cost of the unit has already fallen significantly from what I originally paid and now they want more to get it current, within a year of purchase. Not cool at all. Also, impossible to contact by email. Garmin website is in a permanent loop back to itself when clicking on the "contact by email" option. Otherwise, it's call and wait on hold between certain times. Not cool again.

Then a friend says how well his Verizon GPS works on his wireless phone. I look into that. Verizon offers a full time GPS cost and a single use option for under three bucks per use.

For what I have wasted on this Garmin--over five bills and counting upward forever with their unfriendly updates--that's a whole heck of a lot of one-time Verizon uses with what will be the most updated, most accurate database. After all, no one's going to beat the phone company with accurate phone numbers and addresses.

If I hadn't already bought into the Garmin ripoff, I'd definitely go with Verizon's phone based GPS: the phone will always be with you when you need it instead of in the glove compartment in the other car.

And it most likely won't get stolen. It's a darned pain to have to put the Garmin away after each use so some cretin won't bash in a window to steal a very, very expensive toy that could just as easily fit inside a phone.

Go with the phone.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin nüvi 360 3.5-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Text-To-Speech (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

So far, with the wrapping ear piece, this pair seems to stay on my ears much better than the buds that just pop into the ears. They paired easily to my iPhone and connect automatically each time I take them out of the case. The sound is decent or at least decent enough for me. I do not use these for just listening to music or videos, I have better over the ear headphones for that purpose. For me, I just use these for running, working out or maybe while working around the yard. For that purpose, the sound quality is pretty good. The only suggestion I have is remember to take the clear tape off the charging contacts; I did not realize it was there and my earbuds were not charging each time I put them back in the case. On the upside, I did learn that the battery life is excellent on these earbuds. I cannot say how long they actually lasted before I charged them, but I probably went on 5 or 6 runs before the first ear bud died. With the tape off the contacts, they do charge automatically each time they are placed back in their case. A nice feature is that the case can be charged either with a cord or by setting the case on a charging pad. The price was reasonable. I would recommend these wireless earbuds to anyone looking for a set. Since I cannot fully say how long they will last or how durable they are, I will reserve the 5th star until I have owned these for a while.

Updated 12May21: Ok, I really want to like earbuds, but I cannot. As many times as I have tried earbuds, they just always feel like they are coming out of my ears, even w/the ear wraps on these buds. RUBAN Notebook Lock and Security Cable (PC/Laptop) Two Keys 6.6 Foot (Black) This notebook lock and security cable works with laptops that have a Kensington security slot (about 99% of them on the market do), so it will work for most notebooks except the MacBook Pro. Be sure to check to make sure your laptop has the security port which looks like a small slot usually found in the upper right outside corner.

To use this cable run the end of the cable around a fixed object that can't be moved without effort or drawing attention, such as the leg of a heavy table or a post, then loop the locking end through the loop and attach it to your laptop. The locking mechanism has a built in bar that fits into the Kensington slot, so just insert it into the port, then turn the key 90 degrees to lock it in place. You'll need the key to unlock it when you're ready to take the laptop so be sure to bring it along. When you want to remove your laptop just rotate the key in the opposite direction to unlock it. This set comes with a spare key as well in case you misplace one.

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Chromebook (Wi-Fi, 11.6-Inch) 2012 Model I wanted a computer that was fast and efficient, and didn't bother me with updates all the time. I wanted a device with a keyboard that I could use to surf the Internet, check email, type documents, create to-do lists, update my calendar, and complete quick calculations. I've found all of that and more with Chromebook.

Now, as other reviewers have mentioned, the learning curve might be just a bit steep for those unused to Google's products (besides their search engine, of course). But I'm telling you, once you get the hang of using Google Docs for typing documents, Google slides for creating presentations, Google Calendar for setting dates, etc., you will not want to go back. If you lose your Chromebook or find yourself without it, you can go onto any device that connects to the Internet and find your documents, presentation, calendar, etc.

Technically, you don't even need a Chromebook to use those products, just a Google account. But then you wouldn't have such an efficient, fast machine to use them on--and why would you ever want that?

---------

Just a couple notes on the downsides:

1. Printing is an issue if you don't have a "Cloud Print Ready" printer. Since I don't, my computer scientist husband had to find a work-around.

2. You cannot download external programs. I have to keep my old laptop around for when I want to use iTunes, Blackboard IM (for school), and my scanner. To me, it's no big deal, but don't think that you can use Chromebook for everything because you simply can't. To me, the pros completely outweigh the cons!
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Chromebook (Wi-Fi, 11.6-Inch) 2012 Model

MSI G Series GT70 0ND-219US 17.3-Inch Laptop (Black) PROS: Awesome as advertised! Specs and possibly even the parts blow away most high(er)-end laptops in its class...can't beat it for the price. Was debating this over the Samsung Series 7 Gamer with similar specs and both had similar reviews but MSI performed where it counted the most. Better battery, better cooling, mostly better benchmark tests. A big deciding factor for me was that the older MSI GT70 with GTX660/670 still outperformed and outfeatured the Samsung Series 7 Gamer in most of the benchmarking tests...and this next upgrade to MSI GT70 was only $1850 when I bought it...$30 more that the Samsung at the time.

CONS: My only down was with GPU drivers not the actual laptop itself. I think the drivers are so new not even the supposed "BETA" drivers will work with it. It was almost impossible to find the GTX 675m drivers. NVIDIA recommended I get the drivers from the manufacturer's site. And from what I've found there is only one that works and it is on MSI's website. For some reason when I first looked, MSI, didn't have a "notebook" category in their drivers section. It's not even on NVIDIA's site (this had nothing to do with NVIDIA's forums going down, I checked before there forums got hacked).
My reason for purchase.....
First off, I wanted to get this off my chest because I was planning to build a workstation PC (or a powerful PC) but instead switched to getting a laptop. Being that I'm not a laptop fan, I did extensive weeks of research to find the best laptop I could find for my 3d art/animation and gaming needs. Laptop have always been way overpriced and notebook parts can't even touch the PC counterpart; in terms of performance, cooling, etc. Plus, knowing that this an MSI, helped make my decision because they have a good track record of excellent PC parts. I have been building my own desktop PC's for over 10 years and know you get to enjoy the games and 3d applications the way it was meant to be. Also, I'm in the video game development field and needed a second/backup computer/desktop replacement. My current Intel Q9550/Radeon 5700 1GB/ 8GB DDR2 RAM desktop does the JOB but is getting ancient. I was really thinking about getting a workstation or high-end gaming desktop (which would obviously be way cheaper than the most expensive laptop) but after thinking about it, I liked the idea of having the convenience and portability. And, if my desktop goes belly up one day (as it has been acting up) my work flow pipeline won't take a hit. I wont have to deal with the inconvenience of being in a HOT room with 1000W powersupply... even with air conditioning.

text_fidelity_a:
Soundcore Upgraded, Anker Liberty Neo True Wireless Earbuds, Pumping Bass, IPX7 Waterproof, Secure Fit, Bluetooth 5 Headphones, Stereo Calls, Noise Isolation, One Step Pairing, Sports, Work Out I've used a few other true wireless headphones in the $50 price range (mostly unknown brands) as well as some more expensive brand name models (B&O, Plantronics). This set is better than most headphones in the under $50 price range. Sound is clear and noise free. Volume is loud enough for earbuds, but not booming at full volume. Bass is kind of weak, though that is a common problem in this price range. 3 hour battery life is about average for this price range. Comparing $50 headphones to $100 headphones is not really fair, but if you do want to spend more money, most headphones will give you much better bass and richer overall sound quality. More expensive headphones also give me better battery life (usually at least 4 hours without any recharging). On the other hand, if I'm out running or riding on the subway, I'd rather use these $50 headphones instead of risk losing much more expensive headphones.

I am impressed by the build quality of these Soundcore headphones. They headphones feel solid. They are comfortable in my ears. The case is sleek and the recharging system works well. The buttons that control the headphones work easily and reliably. I do wish they used a modern USB-C charging system instead of the old-fashioned micro-USB.
text_fidelity_b: Soundcore Upgraded, Anker Liberty Neo True Wireless Earbuds, Pumping Bass, IPX7 Waterproof, Secure Fit, Bluetooth 5 Headphones, Stereo Calls, Noise Isolation, One Step Pairing, Sports, Work Out

Travel Adapter, 2400W International All in One Universal Travel Power Plug Adapter, Travel Charger with 1 Type-C / 3 USB Port Adapter Plug, Perfect Adapter for UK, EU, AU, US, Over 170 Countries I have two other adapters very similar to this, but there are a few differences.

Like the other two, this is a little larger than initially expected, but it has to be to have all the built-in adapters. There is still no Italy plug or ground conductor, so this is only ideal if you only have an ungrounded device like a computer (again, without ground) and a few USB-chargeable devices like phones and cameras.

This one has a USB-C port, unlike one of my others, but - unlike the one I have that does have USB-C - the total current is more limited. Both adapters with USB-C ports only support 5v output, so they may not charge your device if your device can only accept higher voltage (USB-C has multiple layers of standards, so can be a bit confusing).

I like this adapter when traveling to multiple regions within one trip. Otherwise, I'll just use the cheap adapters which by themselves are smaller. Out of the three I own, I'm not sure which is best; I think it depends on your personal situation. Hopefully I shared enough to help you decide.

WiFi Video Projector, WEWATCH V10B Wireless Portable Movie Projector with Bluetooth Full HD 1080P Supported Home Theater Video Projector Compatible with HDMI, VGA, TV Stick, iPhone, Android The WEWATCH V30 Portable Projector is a good 1080p projector for its size. I watched some movies with the screen setup to 80-90 inches and the picture looked very good in a dark room. It's important to watch this projector in low ambient lighting due to its low ANSI lumens, as bright light will wash out the picture.

The size of the projector is not as small as the pictures make it seem. Though it is not advertised as a pico projector, I expected it to be smaller. With that said, the projector is not so large that it would be hard to transport or store when not in use.

Unfortunately, I was not able to get the Wi-Fi feature to work with my Iphone. This is not a dealbreaker for me, as I plugged a Roku stick into the HDMI port and the system worked well.

I was surprised by how good the native speakers sound. I found watching movies enjoyable and voices were easy to hear. There are adjustments for the bass and treble levels in the menus. The unit has a headphone jack in the rear which makes hooking up an external speaker set up a breeze.

The fan on the unit is very quiet and is not distracting while it is in use.

While I really like this projector, there is a large downside. The lack of keystone correction is a huge oversight. Placing this projector without keystone adjustment means the projector has to be directly in line with the viewing area making it necessary to use a tripod in most instances. Having to bring a tripod along, makes the unit less portable.

Overall, this is a small projector with a great picture, as long as you can place it in the perfect location without much ambient lighting. If WEWATCH added keystone correction and refined the mirroring feature, this would be a 5 star projector.
text_fidelity_b: WiFi Video Projector, WEWATCH V10B Wireless Portable Movie Projector with Bluetooth Full HD 1080P Supported Home Theater Video Projector Compatible with HDMI, VGA, TV Stick, iPhone, Android

Orion 8923 20mm Expanse Telescope Eyepiece I have an Orion SkyQuest XT6 for over 10 years, and I've only had 3 eyepieces the whole time. Their standard Sirius Plossl 25mm, 17mm and 10mm. For the most part, the 10mm is pretty much useless, as the field of vision is so narrow that constant adjustments need to be made. I decided to give the Expanse series a try. This eyepiece is by far the best in the of the 4. Near Detroit, the light pollution is pretty bad. Viewing the plants and the moon is usually OK. My previous higher powered eyepieces usually made things look really bright and blurry. The Orion Nebula is usually a grey smudge. With the 9mm Expanse, I was able to see more shape to the cloud, and even a handful of stars in its heart. Cloud bands on Jupiter never looked better! I was also able to get a significant amount more detail on the moons surface than what I am used to. Looking at the sun was uneventful today -- only two sunspots.

Ultimately, this is definitely worth buying!

Headphone Adapter Converter Supports Audio and Charging for Motorola MotoZ, Letv ,2 in 1 USB-C to 3.5mm Audio Adapter, Nylon Braided 2 in 1 USB Type C Cable Fast Charge to 3.5mm Audio Jack(Black) This is a much easier alternative to the My K-cup option if you want to use your own coffee in a K-cup machine rather than the pre-packaged cups. Unlike the My K-cup you don't need to remove the inner cup of the machine to use this. It just drops right in, so you can switch between this and a regular k-cup without having to dismantle anything.

The kit is very complete. There are three cups, each a slightly different color (different shades of brown). The cups are decently made. The plastic sides are nice and thick; the o-ring on the cap is of good quality; and the metal mesh is firmly attached. My only quibble with the build quality is the hinge. It's plastic, and I don't have confidence that it will last a long time before breaking. It's not a big deal, since the cup will still work fine even with a broken hinge, so I'm not docking any points due to that potential problem.

I like that the water dispersion channel has slots all around it to ensure water gets sprayed in all directions inside the cup to keep the grounds uniformly wet. I also really like that the lip area has a slight indent to make it very easy to pop open the top with one hand.

It fit fine in my Cuisinart K-cup machine. The lid of the machine was just slightly raised compared with using a "real" k-cup, but it had zero impact on performance. I tried several different brews, all with good results. You will need to fiddle with the grind level to get the best coffee. Too fine of a grind and it gets over-extracted and bitter; too coarse and it's weak.

Cleaning a used cup is very easy. I pop open the top, hold it upside down in the compost pail, and whack it gently on the base with a wooden spoon. Nearly all the used grounds drop out, and what's left can be easily rinsed under running water. You can also just dump the contents into the disposal or garbage if you don't compost your grounds.

Another option is to use a mini filter in the cup. A package of them are included and, while they do make cleanup easier, I prefer to use just the cup without a filter.

The kit also includes a charcoal filter. I didn't use that, so I can't speak to its performance. It looks to be the same size as the filters used in the water intake of my Cuisinart K-cup machine, so I expect it would perform in a similar fashion.

This Smart Cup kit works well, is well-made/designed, and comes in a very complete kit. Having used the My K-cup version I can confidently say that this performs better and is easier to use. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Headphone Adapter Converter Supports Audio and Charging for Motorola MotoZ, Letv ,2 in 1 USB-C to 3.5mm Audio Adapter, Nylon Braided 2 in 1 USB Type C Cable Fast Charge to 3.5mm Audio Jack(Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Canon EF-S 55-250mm f/4.0-5.6 IS II Telephoto Zoom Lens I'm very pleased with this lens given the price. Although it won't give a Canon L lens a run for its money, it's reasonable fast and has a nice range. The build quality is very good for this price point. Both the zoom movement and focusing are smooth. The zoom marking are well-marked. While the mount is plastic rather than metal, this keeps the lens weight down, which is always something that I appreciate. Despite being plastic the mount and housing are more than sturdy enough for even the most avid amateur photographer.

The image stabilization works very well and is an essential feature to have unless you have rock-steady hands.

I find the image quality to be excellent at all zoom ranges except for when it's at its max range, but even then it's more than acceptable.

It's certainly not the best lens that Canon makes, but I don't think there's another zoom out there that can match this performance at this price. It's a great second lens if you have a crop sensor body (such as the Rebel series) and the 18-55mm zoom (which is a common kit lens). The pair provides a wide range of shooting opportunities at a very reasonable cost. Highly recommend.
text_fidelity_b: Canon EF-S 55-250mm f/4.0-5.6 IS II Telephoto Zoom Lens

once in movies, I should be able to search for a movie by name from this point.

I ought to be able to then say, what's going on for the 14th. And it should be the 14th. I should be able to say, add event for the 14th and then add the event. I know, rocket science, right?

text_fidelity_a:
EarStudio ES100 MK2-24bit Portable High-Resolution Bluetooth Receiver/USB DAC/Headphone Amp with LDAC, aptX HD, aptX, AAC (3.5mm Unbalanced & 2.5mm Balanced Output) Very nice features, sounds great, 2.5 balanced output! BT v5, aptXHD, top of the line DAC’s, great battery life. So why just 4 stars? The documentation leaves a lot to be desired. The included printed doc was about the size of a matchbook with writing so small it required a magnifying glass to read and for all that effort it basically said nothing. The biggest hassle was the pairing. It couldn’t be less intuitive. I have many BT devices, both receivers and transmitters and this is the first one that required a web search to figure out. Very frustrating. And to enable the BT v5 it requires a ROM flash upgrade so you have to connect it to a PC and follow a bunch of steps that are as intuitive as the pairing. I came within seconds of sending it back but stuck it out because it had some pretty stellar reviews. It turns out I’m glad I did. Once you get it sorted out it is a pretty amazing piece of kit. I use it with my HiBy r6 and BGVP DMG’S as well as my ATH M-50x headphones. I can now roam freely around the kitchen while keeping the DAP safely out of the way. I can plug-in the 2.5mm balanced cable and get outstanding sound with the added bonus of not heating up the DAP (it gets hot when plugged in directly) and the battery life of the HiBy is more than doubled. Both of these bonuses more than make up for the minor degradation in sound staging. I have listened for over 7 hours without the battery giving up, but have not used it up to it’s limit yet so I can’t say how long it will last. Is it worth the Benjamin it cost? Oh yeah.

Update: Upgraded to 5 stars after a month of use. Once the niggling little details were figured out and the unit was set up I can't say enough good things about this puppy. My main reason for getting a BT transmitter was I am going to be doing extensive bicycle touring later this year and since it will be solo touring I wanted good quality music available. I have an extensive library of 24 bit flac's as well as a couple of hundred audiobooks for the trip and while the playback of the books isn't important the music is. I invested a fair amount of cash into a HiBy R6 DAP and BGVP DMG IEM's as well as upgraded cables to connect them. The EarStudio lets me connect via 2.5" balanced with no real discernible degredation in the quality of the playback as opposed to plugging directly into the output on the DAP, and here's the kicker, instead of just getting 6 - 7 hours of playback and heating up the DAP I now get double that without any heat. I can stash the HiBy in a Pelican 1020 case and put it in my top tube bag where it's out of harms way and protected in case of misadventure. The EarStudio has a battery life of around 14 hours (I haven't run it out yet, and I have listened for over 8 hours). Added to that the App that is available for my Android based DAP is amazing. More fiddly bits than your above average geek could ever want. So I gotta give it a 5 star rating. And it's worth twicw the price but don't tell Radsone.
text_fidelity_b: EarStudio ES100 MK2-24bit Portable High-Resolution Bluetooth Receiver/USB DAC/Headphone Amp with LDAC, aptX HD, aptX, AAC (3.5mm Unbalanced & 2.5mm Balanced Output)

text_fidelity_a:
TCL 65" Class 4-Series 4K UHD HDR Roku 2017 Smart TV - 65S405 Do not be afraid! This is a great TV.

The good: I won't go into the technical details and explanations. Others have done that for me. We purchased this for a new home and have had it set up for a couple of weeks. The integration of Roku is seamless, and it retains those same intuitive menus. It has no WiFi connectivity issues for us (we have a Google mesh network with a good signal at the TV location), and effortlessly streams Netflix, Amazon Video and You TubeTV-- DVR and live-- and looks great doing it. I haven't tried 4K content yet, so can't comment on that.

The bad: It doesn't handle low light scenes very well in movies and television, and particularly when viewed from any angle that isn't straight on. That's why I gave it four stars instead of five. If you can overcome that, forge ahead! I couldn't justify spending twice or more on Samsung or others. Another minor quibble-- silver feet on a black frame looks a little odd.

The bottom line: I was skeptical. I've owned Samsung plasma and LED and an LG LED recently and I see no material difference between the TCL and the other LEDs. All the positive reviews here, plus the CNet reviews/primers on Roku integrated TVs put me over the edge. We really like this TV and it's simplified our streaming incredibly. Go get it!
text_fidelity_b: TCL 65" Class 4-Series 4K UHD HDR Roku 2017 Smart TV - 65S405

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Kindle Fire HD 8.9" Standing Leather Case, Fuchsia (will not fit HDX models) This case fits very well and was designed specifically for the Kindle Fire HD 8.9"—with even slick cutouts for the speakers in the back. The Fire just pops right into it and it couldn't be neater or slimmer. The magnetic closure is tidy and holds the case closed quite well. I think Amazon must be trying to recoup some from its bargain-level pricing of its Kindles, however, because I think it's over-priced for what it is (at least at the time of this writing). Still, you can't beat the fit of it.

But a caution is in order for the leather lovers: This may be "genuine leather" but it sure doesn't look or feel like it. If you get it in black or the Saddle Tan, maybe, but the one I was given to review (fuschia) just looks like fancy plastic to me. It has a pebbly texture that makes it easy to hold, but if you want that rich, satisfying feel of well-worn wallet leather, you won't get it with this case. (The Verso Prologue cases have that feel.)

As with so many of the Kindle cases on the market, the inability to clip a stylus to the case is I think an omission. I have a rooCase for my Kindle Fire 7" that I like specifically because I can clip my stylus to the pocket that holds the Kindle. Maybe some hot new designer will come up with a way to design a very slim case that can stow a stylus.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Kindle Fire HD 8.9" Standing Leather Case, Fuchsia (will not fit HDX models)

text_fidelity_a:
Sony X800H 55-inch TV: 4K Ultra HD Smart LED TV with HDR and Alexa Compatibility - 2020 Model Background: I spec and integrate the highest resolution LCD’s produced in aerospace defense applications. LCD image performance is measured in hundreds of dimensions and environments. Sony is not a player in that space.

For home, I’ve been SID show and showroom shopping LCD, OLEDs, etc image quality for years. This year, I’m replacing a comparably sized exercise room 1080p LCD set. Sony has always been, to my eye, a superb comparative model and a $100 or so more than other competitors. Is the premium worth it?

This Sony X800H is an eye grabber across the showroom and on close inspection. It’s a phenomenal picture. Sony’s proprietary LCD foundries are unique in the industry. The Sony LCD foundry produces a distinctive LCD that is worth the premium price to the discerning.

Performance-wise, Sony reduced the native refresh rate to 60hz from 120hz last year. That’s quite practical as it will be some years before >60fps cameras are widely available at native 120fps. No matter, the 60hz to 120hz refresh is not discernible to the eye. The X800H imaging software can be seen to take care of latency artifacts at factory default settings … no viewing distance ghosting, inverse ghosting, blur or pulse-width modulation.

There is a comment regarding darkness, edge lighting, and illumination issues. The X800H is both edge and background light as best as I can discern without tearing it apart. It's uniform lighting no matter. Sony has always been the master of the best 'optical black' pixel to enrich the color pixel perception. The X800H is loaded with image quality controls. text_fidelity_a:
Phaiser BHS-750 Bluetooth Headphones Headset Sport Earphones with Mic and Lifetime Sweatproof Guarantee - Wireless Earbuds for Running, Redheat 3-day update: After trying many tips I'm still not overly impressed. I found I got the best fit with the wire over rear but the mic keeps them from being practical over-ear and the angle of the wire on the other side with the tip at the best angle for kept making the wire come off my ear. In not a fan of comply tips but I finally tried them as a last resort and the sound did improve. But in the end, my theory is that I just can't get these deep enough in my ear due to the large housing to get some bass to balance out the brightness. But even if it did I find the mid-range to lack warmth and certain aspect of the sound to be harsh.

First impression - not as impressed as some

Disclaimer: Everyone's ear is different, and tips make a big difference. Because of my ears, I have to use big tips and a shallow fit. Those who can get a deeper fit my hear something completely different. Also, I'm being really picky to help others decide if this is the right phones for them.

I wanted to try these on my computer because that is where all my music is stored that I've used for decades to audition audio gear. So this will be based on Pandora on my phone at 192kb. This is fine because this is how I will be listening to them.

I could not get a comfortable fit with the included tips. The largest tips were not large enough for my ears. So I dug through my collection and found a good fit. Pairing went fine.

They feel a little heavy to me but maybe that is the price of Bluetooth and the magnets? This is my first pair of Bluetooth in-ears. Build quality seem good for the price (I got them on sale) and I'd say the build quality is about average for their normal selling price. While they look like they have good strain relief it's actually very stiff plastic creating a 'hard point' where the wires come out. I like the little magnet for when I want to take them out but not take them off. It's one of the reasons I got these. If you run, I'd worry a little bit about the weight they add.

The sound. I like tight bass, well controlled, no extra bloom/extension But these are bass shy to my ears. For a workout, I like a fun sound and these ain't that. They are a bit bright and brassy at times I noticed the most on 70s classic rock. They lack a richness in the mids that I noticed most with male vocals. Turning them up did not improve they sound, as they got louder they became painful bright/brassy and bass did not improve. They went loud enough to distort the drivers so volume should not be an issue for anyone.

They do a pretty good job of revealing detail and room acoustics are rendered decently and there is some space around the instruments but not much of a soundstage.

While not sterile they lack some musicality that I'd prefer. Did I mention that male voice sound thin. They lack a fullness and resonance for the male voice. I notice this lack of 'something' on drums as well which are buried in the mix. It seems like the SQ is geared to making them sound impressive and accurate and while they succeed in that to some extent it's at the expense of other parts of the sound. I can see getting some fatigue after a while if you listen for more than an hour or so. Sibilance is not an issue. You hear the sibilance on some songs because it's there but it's not going to wear you out.

I can see why some people would like these especially if you are coming from lower quality mushy sounding earphones. If you are used to better earphones and looking for some less expensive earphones for working out you may like these if you like a 'clear' sound but the word that keeps coming to mind as I listen to them more and more is 'thin'. Not thin/thin but a lack of richness and resonance. If you want some bass especially some extension/bloom (again wearing/tips can make a difference) and a bit of 'drive' I'd consider a different set.
text_fidelity_b: Phaiser BHS-750 Bluetooth Headphones Headset Sport Earphones with Mic and Lifetime Sweatproof Guarantee - Wireless Earbuds for Running, Redheat

- I do think the read aloud smarts have been improved since the older model (kbd) as it reads much cleaner now for me. (Less stops, more in the right locations, etc).

My end-game is that I will probably return it. If it does not work reliably on battery then it is not a mobile device. Period.

They come with several options for improving fit. I settled on some of the bigger flappy looking parts as being very comfortable. Unfortunately, after wrestling them onto the earbuds, I found that the lid is no longer even close to closing on the charging case. I'd call it an inexcusable design oversight. Lots of tuning options in the app.

Compared to other earbuds I've tried, they sound better and are much heavier than much less expensive brands, but I'm not sure it's worth it. At similar price points, I've tried two other brands. One was even bigger, but sounded amazing (Bose), and the other I found to be superior in nearly every way.

text_fidelity_a:
SanDisk Sansa Fuze 4 GB Video MP3 Player (Black) SanDisk has come out with an extension to their array of MP3 players, beyond the Clip and the View. Their new mp3 player, the Sansa Fuze, is definitely geared towards casual someone who just wants a basic, functional, and well-put together media device for their pocket.

The Sansa Fuze may look like a tiny device at first, but this thing packs some serious features. It has the ability to playback music, video, photos, FM radio, as well as audiobooks. The features for the Sansa Fuze are very impressive to say the least, as it also features a microSD card slot to add extra storage space, content, etc.

The first feature we will focus on is the one which will likely get the most use, the audio aspect. The music menu is organized with artist, album, song, genre, etc. There is also a recently added section which shows the most recent songs added onto the device, as well as a top rated section.

The album menu allows you to see album icons as you are scrolling through the various albums. There is also the ability to form a playlist directly on the player.

The sound quality is very well-done. If you have a great set of headphones you will not be disappointed in the least bit.

The video aspect is definitely not the highlight of the Sansa Fuze. Part of this is due to the low power of the device, and partly due to the screen itself. The supplied Sansa Media Converter does make it easy to convert movies into a format for the device though. A typical movie will take up a little under, or over 1GB. The video looks respectable, but can get a bit choppy at times. One very cool feature about the video is the ability to add a bookmark while watching it.

The photo viewer is very standard as you can view photos from the internal memory of a microSD card. You can set up a slide show with time intervals, and add music as well. The images looked quite sharp.

The FM radio feature is done extremely well on the Sansa Fuze. You get some great reception and the auto program feature picks out crystal clear radio stations. It also has the ability to record radio in WAV format.

This works with voice recording as well thanks to a microphone located right below the microSD slot.

Podcasts and audiobooks are pretty self-explanatory, but one issue with the audiobooks is the lack of a bookmark feature.

The overall user interface for the Sansa Fuze is put together nicely, set up in such a way that a first-time user could pick up this device and feel right at home with it. You have a scroll wheel as well as a home button and a middle click wheel. The scroll wheel can also be clicked up and down, which can make things a bit confusing at times. Overall though, beyond a few hiccups with organizational aspects of the UI, this is one easy device to use.

Getting media onto the Sansa Fuze is extremely simple as you can use any desktop media player to create playlists and such, easily syncing them to the device. It also supports drag and drop without the need for any software. We used Windows Media Player as well as a few other media players to test this all out, and syncing was as simple as can be.

The quality of the device itself is top-notch, as the screen can put out some great contrast and vibrant colors in spots. The screen is extremely clear and does a nice job with photo presentations. Battery life is equally as impressive, as I have been getting around 20 hours on each battery charge thus far. Video playback came in at around 6 hours on a charge.

The package comes with a proprietary USB cable and a pair of earbuds, pretty basic.

Also shipping with the Sansa Fuze is a great bonus, a microSD card which comes with DRM-free music from more than 50 new and emerging artists. This is a great way to immediately test out the music capabilities of the Sansa Fuze, and also adds value to the entire package. Music videos, images, and more are also included on the microSD card.

Overall SanDisk has done a great job with the Sansa Fuze.
text_fidelity_b: SanDisk Sansa Fuze 4 GB Video MP3 Player (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm Finepix F70EXR 10MP Super CCD Digital Camera with 10x Optical Dual Image Stabilized Zoom and 2.7 inch LCD This is a high quality camera, but you must take time to read through the owner's manual to understand how to get the best pictures. You can just grab it and point and shoot using it while in the "automode" setting, but the resulting pictures may leave you a little disappointed depending upon the photographic conditions. To get the highest quality photos you must become familiar with how this little beauty works. Unfortunately, you might have to print out and tote the manual with you when you find yourself in situations where your pictures aren't what you'd like, or you can't figure out how to do certain things like know what's behind the flashing icon error message, or how to simulate different types of film, or can you choose between clarity, reduced noise and dynamic range? This is not really a simple "point and shoot" camera and all images will turn out great. You will have to study it, practice with it, and most of all have patience and you will be pleasantly rewarded for your efforts. Though the indicators vary with camera settings, there are 23 different indicators just for shooting mode, and 12 for playback mode, not to mention the date/time stamp, battery level, and indicator. It can get confusing.

Although a basic manual booklet is included with the camera, a much more detailed manual must be uploaded from the enclosed CD and then all 125 pages can be printed out or read from your computer monitor. The manual covers all the material in the booklet almost page for page but includes much more information about features the booklet leaves out and the booklet will refer you to specific pages in the manual for more information. Also, in the manual are about 50 FAQ's that are very useful. I am a manual reader, (having written many technical SOP's) and appreciate having well-written and well thought out manuals that are understandable and succinct. Though I would have preferred a manual that I don't have to upload to my computer, it is well-written and many useful pictures are included.

This camera is loaded with many different options/features but accessing and understanding many of them will require reading the manual. For people who don't want to be bothered with all the bells and whistles this camera may be more than they need. I can see very serious photographers using this camera. Reading through the manual I have compiled a list of some of the various modes, options and features available:

Digital Zoom
Movie Mode
Silent Mode
Variable ISO settings
Image size selection
Aspect Ratio selection
Intelligent Face detection
Scene Position
Shooting Modes
EXR Mode
Film simulation
Dynamic Range
White Balance
Continuous Photography
Photometry - multi, spot, average

Playback Options:
Erase
Slide Show
Red-eye Removal
Image Rotation
Protection from accidental deletion
Crop
Resize
Voice Memo
Print Order
Time Difference
Format

Pages 37, 67-68, 86-87, 97-103, and 104-107 would be good to print out and keep with your camera as they contain tables of various camera functions and a trouble shooting chart.

I have taken many pictures and movies inside and out, light and dark, with this camera set on various settings. And though I have practiced with it now for several weeks, I still need to often refer to the manual when I choose to vary from automode. Some things I have found especially desirable are:

Silent Mode - I attend classical music concerts where flash photography is prohibited. This mode will silence all beeps and flashes.

Large viewing screen on the back of the camera. It is exactly 5.5cm x 4.0 cm.

Digital Zoom - extremely good. I attended a local minor-league baseball game and sat far away on the grass well beyond the playing field. I was able to fully zoom and still get good, clear, close-up shots of the players with no blurring.

Movie Mode - Completely surpasses any other I've experienced so far. Images are clear, colorful and the sound quality is excellent. Camera noise was heard and recorded while using the "zoom" function in Movie Mode though it was not very loud.

Multi-frame play back function is very useful to quickly scan for a particular picture.

Fine Pix Viewer Program was very easy to install on my computer. I use Windows XP.

Very good photography in low-light conditions.

Also some things I did not find particularly desirable but are not major flaws:

I cannot directly burn a CD using the Fine Pix Viewer Program which comes with this camera. I have to use another camera program, import the pictures into it and then burn a CD.

Very easy to accidentally turn it on or off and easy to get misfires.

The zoom lever is too sensitive. I have learned with practice to barely move it very slowly.

The camera does not give helpful suggestions on how to get a better picture as does my HP R717.

Not HD capable.

The higher the ISO the grainier the picture though a higher ISO is desirable when shooting in dim/low light levels. I have set the ISO level to 200 and that seems to produce the best pictures so far.

Almost too many options, modes and functions to choose from. Though you can immediately begin to take pictures using Automode, it will take time to fully understand the many other aspects and features this camera has.

In Summary:

I can find no major complaint concerning this camera. It takes excellent clear and colorful photos even in situations where I least expect it - indoors with no flash. Any poor quality pictures I have taken are not the fault of the camera but due to the photographer's ignorance of how to use/understand properly the many features of the camera. The basic mechanics of such things as battery and memory card installation are very easy. Battery charging is a very simple process and battery life seems long. The manual is detailed and covers more than I would probably care to know. This is almost more camera than I need, though I will continue to use it and will update this review as necessary.

UPDATE 2.9.15 - Been using this camera all these years and now it's beginning to show it's age and giving me some problems. The viewing screen on the back has a vertical big black bar but it doesn't appear on the actual pictures. And the lens cover doesn't always completely open when the camera is turned on. I still use it but it might be time to think about a replacement. It's been good though so I really don't have any complaints.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm Finepix F70EXR 10MP Super CCD Digital Camera with 10x Optical Dual Image Stabilized Zoom and 2.7 inch LCD

Sony SRS-XB21 Portable Wireless Bluetooth Speaker, Black (SRSXB21/B) A very impressive looking speaker. The unit has good heft to it and if feels sturdy and it is exceptionally well constructed. It also sounds really good. At full volume it can easily fill a decent sized room with sound, the bass is clear, with great mid range and wonderful highs.

That being said, the speaker does have a lot of things wrong with it. First, the USB cable that comes with it is very short. It also doesn’t come with a power adapter, so you have to have an extra one around, which shouldn’t be a problem, but at this price, this speaker should come with a power adapter.

There are white lights on the front that bounce and light up and pulse to the music. Very cool for a party, but grows old quick. I was hoping to take this camping, but I don’t want dancing lights when I’m out in the woods. I can’t seem to find a way to turn them off. The instructions are very sparse and not helpful at all.

Even plugged in there is a unit time out where it powers down after so many minutes. I was hoping this would be a good external speaker for my Amazon Echo Dot, but that won’t work.

It also is supposed to have a feature where you tap (more like hit hard) the speaker for sounds like a high hat, cymbal, and Tom Tom. when it works, it’s pretty cool, but it seemed to only work intermittently. And in order for it to sound any good at all, you have to hit it very hard.

Connecting to it is easy. You can connect through your phone’s Bluetooth or tap your phone on it, if it has NFC, for even easier connections. It also has a aux port for connecting with an aux wire. Battery lasts a long time.

Overall it’s a good sounding speaker, and it’s well made. But be warned, depending on what you want it for, this may not be for you. The lights that won’t shut off and the unit time off (even when on external power) as well as the short power cable make me not recommend it to many people.

I used a dB meter that was about 6ft away with the speaker pointed towards the meter. At max volume on my main phone (fold3) and at 150% volume, I was getting a consistent mid-90s dB for melody and lyrics, with peaks up to 109dB. On my other device (Note 10+), also at 150%, it was pulling about 70 dB on TV dialogue. I did try testing it with a volume booster, and even with only 110% (on top of the 150%) it was beginning to distort.
I played the TV audio for about 16hrs at moderate and 8hrs on low, and it was reading as still having 70% battery. But after only a few hours of moderate-high volume music, that 70% was gone and it died.
The sound quality is quite good with a warm tone. The highs are clear and the bass is better than I expected for there not to be a dedicated bass cone.
Despite appearances, I think the best use for this will be background music - not too loud will keep it playing all day & night and it will provide a much cleaner and richer sound than a small speaker at similar volume.

text_fidelity_a:
GAOMON PD2200 130% sRGB Full-Laminated Pen Display with 8192 Battery-Free Tilt-Support Stylus 8 Touch Buttons -21.5'' Graphics Drawing Tablet Monitor with Adjustable Stand I am a huge supporter of open source graphics software because I feel that the leading brand name software uses their virtual monopoly to bully people into overpriced, restrictive, nonsensical subscription programs. When I saw that this tablet was listed as being compatible with GIMP and most other graphics programs, I felt comfortable purchasing it for my uses.

However, upon installing it, I found that it is not actually compatible with the vast majority of graphic software except for those supported by Adobe, and a couple of other inferior programs. To clarify, it will still "function" with most programs, but only as a basic mouse. It will not support pressure sensitivity nor tilt. This, in my mind, means that it is NOT compatible, as pressure and tilt are essential functions for any illustrator. Without them, this is basically just a glorified mouse pad.

From Gaomon's troubleshooting website regarding lack of pressure sensitivity:

"The version of your drawing program might be too low to support pen pressure. Please upload it or try to draw in other drawing programs. Here do we suggest you some drawing programs. For windows system: Adobe Photoshop CC, Adobe Photoshop CC 2015, Adobe Photoshop CC 2017, Adobe Photoshop CC 2018, Adobe Photoshop cs5，Adobe Photoshop cs6, Adobe Animate CC2017 For Mac system: Adobe Photoshop CC, Adobe Photoshop CC 2015, Adobe Photoshop CC 2017, Adobe Photoshop cs5, Adobe Photoshop cs6, Adobe illustrator cs6, Adobe Flash Professional CC, Adobe Animate CC 2018 Other free drawing programs: Sai, Krita, FireAlpaca"

Contrast that with the information in the product listing, which says, "compatible with most of major drawing software such as Photoshop、SAI version 2、Illustrator、krita、firealpaca、gimp、SketchBook Pro、MediBang Paint Pro, etc."

GIMP and others are clearly listed, but are not actually compatible. This is highly misleading.

As for other aspects of the tablet, I can't say too much as I haven't used it very much due to this issue. However, from what I have found so far, the display looks good, and the set up is pretty straightforward, although their manual is extremely confusing to try to follow.

The buttons on the side of the display are completely smooth and can not be felt; there is nothing there to help you locate them by tactile means, so you will have to stop looking at your work and visually find them in order to use them. They are also located such that they are easily pressed accidentally when adjusting the position of your tablet, which gets annoying pretty quickly.

The chords that come with the tablet are a bit short, maybe 4 or 5 feet, which doesn't allow for much room to position your tablet if you use a PC that is located beneath your desk or to the side, especially if the hook-up ports are on the back of the PC. You can of course buy replacement chords.

The stylus is very lightweight, which I personally consider a positive but some people may prefer a heftier stylus.

There is not much lag when using the stylus; the movement is smooth enough for my needs. The pressure sensitivity, when tested in a diagnostic program, seems quite good as well. It just doesn't work with the software I hoped to use it with.

Overall the tablet is a nice size and has a nice display, but the other issues are factors you should consider when deciding between this tablet and a more expensive brand.
text_fidelity_b: GAOMON PD2200 130% sRGB Full-Laminated Pen Display with 8192 Battery-Free Tilt-Support Stylus 8 Touch Buttons -21.5'' Graphics Drawing Tablet Monitor with Adjustable Stand

text_fidelity_a:
Schlage WCE100 Home Indoor Camera with Nexia Home Intelligence, White This is the best overview of the components I've seen so far:

Nexia Home Bridge (this is the key component)
Schlage touch screen deadbolt w alarm
Schlage home keypad lock
Schlage home dimmer/appliance module
Schlage home indoor camera
Schlage home outdoor camera
Trane home energy management thermostat
American Standard AccuLink((tm)) remote thermostat
Trane ComfortLink ((tm)) II Control
American Standard AccuLink((tm)) Platinum ZV control (?)
Schlage home door/window sensor
Schlage home motion sensor
Other Z-Wave sensor
Other Z-Wave thermostat
Other Z-Wave lighting device
Other Z-Wave wall switch and outlet

They might have considered making the 9V battery compartment in the "Bridge" just a little bit bigger. It's a mighty snug fit and you have to remove the battery to get the MAC ID. In fact, you have to remove the 9V battery so often it's a curiosity why the battery door is such a pain to remove and why the battery is so difficult to get out of its little bay. I was actually using a flat screwdriver to pry the battery out, it's that tight.

---

Overall, now that the camera, light dimmer and lock and installed, "enrolled" and apparently functional..? WHAT A GREAT SYSTEM!!! The components look great, they're top-quality. Now that I see everything in action (especially video of my home on my iPhone) the subscription fee seems like not such a high price to pay for what you're getting. I know that I'm going to be sorely tempted to add more cameras.

The deadbolt operates with a passcode OR with a physical key. At first I was thinking that you could lock yourself out accidentally but after examining the lock and playing with the buttons I see that is not the case.

I also understand why the light dimmer module goes so well with the indoor camera -- when it gets dark, you'd want to be able to ramp up the light enough for the camera to see! It's a temptation to put the indoor camera in one of my kids room, which is what I might have done when they were small. That would be a rude intrusion these days. So it's outside a hallway that all traffic must pass through. The field of vision nearly covers the two main doors into and out of our home, also. So I can keep an eye on who's getting home when and all that parent-of-teenagers type stuff.

Is there a controller for exterior lights? Or some kind of interface that would allow me to remotely control wired exterior lights?

The only downside to this system, aside from the kludge-y installation process, is that you will want to add more components, and they aren't cheap.

Bottom line: top-quality components, frustrating "enrollment" process -- once you get it all up and running, it's quite impressive. It's nearly worth the frustration to see it all in operation. It would be nice if you could pan-and-zoom the camera. Perhaps that will be forthcoming in another camera model.

I can't help but feel that the process of "enrolling" the components couldn't be made more simple or more streamlined.

Now to budget for an exterior camera... maybe two...

---

Now that I've seen the system in operation I grasp what the manufacturer is actually offering -- remote control of your home administered via your iPhone or iPad. Ideal for working professionals. Getting everything connected and communicating was a little effort, but it's really a beautiful system in operation. You will definitely want to add more light controls and cameras, at least I would. I wonder if there's an exterior light module? There must be. Once you see it in operation the subscription will not be an issue. You are getting more than what you're paying for.

An excellent upgrade to your home and a clever way to keep tabs on a vacation home.
text_fidelity_b: Schlage WCE100 Home Indoor Camera with Nexia Home Intelligence, White

text_fidelity_a:
Jaybird Freedom Sprint Bluetooth Headphones - Retail Packaging - Midnight Black Overall I'm very pleased with these ear buds. They are my first pair of bluetooth buds and it has been wonderful to not have to deal with cords, especially when working out. I can't tell you how many times I've hit an earbud cord while exercising and ripped the ear bud from my ear. A real pain in the neck (and ear!).

>>>Pros:

Comfort - These fit very well in my ear. There are different tip sizes to create a good fit and, after trying them all out, I went with the medium size. Very comfortable to wear even for long periods of time.

Stay put - I've yet to have them fall out even when doing aerobic exercises or while on the treadmill.

Sound - they sound pretty good. The sound is not as good as my favorite (and inexpensive) corded buds ([[ASIN:B0053R0WWG RHA MA-350 Aluminium Noise Isolating In-Ear Earphones]]) but they are a solid B+ performer with regard to bass response and overall clarity. Keep in mind that good bass response is affected by how the buds fit in your ear, so it's important to try out different tip sizes to see how they affect sound quality. They do get harsh at loud volumes, but for normal listening they are more than fine for my non-audiophile ears. They do reasonably well at blocking out ambient noise.

Setup - I found it straightforward even though I've never had any experience with setting up bluetooth earbuds.

Size - nice and compact so you don't get the "radar dish" look that larger units can have.

Durability - they have a "sweat proof" guarantee which is nice (although I imagine, like most guarantees, there are some loopholes). Overall build quality is good, with a very solid feel to all components.

>>>Cons:

Battery life - The manufacturer claims a battery life of 4.5 hours but I've yet to get more than 3 hours off a single charge. Plus there's no warning about battery life (until you're almost fully discharged) or a visual indicator of how much charge there is left.

Usability - the buttons on the buds are too small, making it difficult for me to push the right one. A lot of fumbling and mis-presses, making it often easier to deal with volume changes on the device, which kills some of the value of having wireless buds. I guess I lack the nimble fingers of the primary target market.

But overall, I'm pleased. The pros outweigh the cons, and I think this is a solid 4-star device.
text_fidelity_b: Jaybird Freedom Sprint Bluetooth Headphones - Retail Packaging - Midnight Black

text_fidelity_a: Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st) The new Kindle arrived within 2 days of my order. I sat down and played around with it for a few minutes and learned the icons but that's all that can be done until it is registered with Amazon. I took it to Toyota while getting my car serviced. Our local Toyota dealer has free WiFi for customers. The Kindle found the hot spot and Amazon recognized the Kindle right away.  It took a few taps around the screen to get started but was easy with a little exploring. Within the time to get an oil change, I had downloaded my ebooks from Cloud and even bought a nice app on sale.  Next I stopped by BestBuy and added a Kindle micro USB to USB cable.  The cable can be used to download ebooks from your PC when not connected to wireless.  Using free Calibre to manage the free ebooks from the Internet, enables covers and metadata for those ebooks that have none.  Calibre will also download the books to Kindle from a PC.  The Fire is great but took some thinking and patience to get it to do all the things I imagined it would do. For instance, ebooks without covers will all look alike and have no title.  This is why it is important to use Calibre for ebook management. Reading ebooks is so much better than it was 10 years ago and this is only the beginning.  The download speed is great.  The reading speed is also great.The storage space is really more than enough.  The 8 Gigabytes of memory is close to 2 warehouses of data.  I read that somewhere on Wikipedia in the middle of the night.  To put it in proportion, imagine having up to 6000 books in your home. The Kindle does not get hot like a netbook and is smaller and lighter too.  The battery life is much better than my 7" netbook also.  Like other customers, I would have liked the micro USB to USB cable included in the box.  3G would be great too.  The best thing about Kindle Fire is the color.  The color is as beautiful as everyone says it is.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st)

text_fidelity_a:
Echo (3rd Gen)- Smart speaker with Alexa- Charcoal I'm not paranoid (famous last words). No, really, I welcome my personal assistant overlords. My family is pretty vanilla. So it only creeps me out a little when my husband and I have "test" discussions about things we don't talk about, don't search the internet for, and would never actually buy in a million years only to see such items pushed to us in advertising feeds. Is one of our assistants listening when it is supposed to be asleep? If so, which one? All three of the majors are in our house. Both of the cats have turned Siri on by walking across my laptop. And Alexa hears her name sometimes inexplicably. Maybe it's my husband's Long Island accent?

Or maybe it is just randomness and the assistants are functioning as advertised. Either way, I won't be getting rid of them anytime soon. The Echo Plus recognized all but two of my smart bulbs and found all of my switches and everything else that still works (old WeMo stuff went offline over a year ago when Belkin pushed a firmware upgrade and killed their wifi connections). It has controlled them flawlessly so far, and this has allowed me to free up the ethernet ports I'd dedicated to several different hubs.

My Echo devices are the ones we use most around here, both because the house runs on Amazon Prime and Subscribe and Save (I have lupus and cannot easily shop in the real world) AND because the Echos allow me to reach my teenager and tell him things whether he wants to hear them or not. He can ignore my texts and refuse to answer the phone, but Alexa lets me yell at him from anywhere in the world. (And the app lets me see his history of ridiculous teenaged boy questions - unlike Siri, Alexa is not a potty mouth and does not like it when you are.)

On the downside, Alexa won't give you suggestions if she doesn't know something. She just gives you an Elizabeth Jennings (The Americans) type, "Hmmm," and a disappointed note.

The Echo Plus also seems to "hear" better and have fewer false activations. And the sound is better for music - by a surprising amount. So, if Alexa has a place in your home, the Echo Plus is a good way to get her. Four stars. I'd give five if the wake word were more customizable.
text_fidelity_b: Echo (3rd Gen)- Smart speaker with Alexa- Charcoal

I wanted to put a set of headphones up on this rack. But it never happened. Sure, they would stick, and hold. But then, when other cables would be attached, and detached, the headphones would fall. But cords, are a rock solid stick.
And it is pretty. I’m no designer, but I think it makes my desk look like I care. And it’s a conversation piece. I really like this piece. But I still think, I should have thought of this.

Ring Video Doorbell (1st Gen) – 720p HD video, motion activated alerts, easy installation – Satin Nickel I'm an early adopter of lots of "smart everything" internet connected products (Nest stuff, Smart Grill, SmartVents, internet connected cars, etc.). I have found the Ring doorbell to be one of the most useful and reliable of these types of products. Remote functions that are really valuable to me:
* Remotely "greet" and reschedule the delivery guy who was 2 hours late, while you are out doing other other errands. Warning - it does really freak out most delivery guys to hear your voice emanating from the doorbell button !
* Receive confirmation that your tween/teen has made it home from school, even when they don't see fit to call or text. Plus do a body count to see if any "extras" are visiting. Plus also have a concrete, time-stamped log of any late night returns, so you don't have to stay up late to intercept returning teens.
* Capture video evidence of stolen packages, unwanted solicitations, and prowlers.
The cloud recording cost of 30$/yr is a far better value than other services like Next or Flir. Ring is the clear choice for door monitoring as well as a really cool doorbell.

My only caveats for buyers:
* Take care with the physical installation on very rough surfaces like rough stucco. Holes need to exactly align (no slotted mounting holes) plus the mount plate is sensitive to bending. If the most bends too much to conform to the wall, the actual button/bell unit will not attach.
* Make sure your WiFi signal is strong enough in the location where you are planning install the ring. Plaster and stucco (with embedded screening) attenuate WiFi signals. WiFi basestation with beam-forming really do help (one of my neighbors needed to swap an Apple Airport Express for an Airport Extreme Basestation to achieve reliable and no-laggy video, but now the Ring works like a charm)
* Make sure your transformer is putting out an in-spec voltage, for a wired installation. Mine worked fine, but the another neighbor who recommended the Ring to me wen through two units (replaced by Ring), before they determined the doorbell voltage from the transformer was too high. Things worked flawlessly with the third unit when my neighbor moved to unwired operation.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell (1st Gen) – 720p HD video, motion activated alerts, easy installation – Satin Nickel

I always wonder why products allow you to raise the volume far beyond the limits of what the product can sustain without creating distortion. The point at which the product does this is roughly halfway; it can only go to roughly 65-80 decibels before treble starts to sound horrible, distorted, and messy. That is NOT very loud at all. The sound, even at lower volumes, is somewhat fuzzy: you cannot hear detail in the music like you can with better quality speakers. Even With the distortion, at maximum volume, it doesn't get Very loud. That's mostly to be expected at this price point and in something of this size with rechargeable batteries, you can't hope for much more than this product has to offer. Samsung Electronics 840 EVO-Series 120GB 2.5-Inch SATA III Single Unit Version Internal Solid State Drive MZ-7TE120BW As of early 2014, this is the price/value drive to get, for a home system.

Yeah there is another drive that is as good for the same money, just sort on #of reviews or rating to have it come up. But this and that one are can't miss price/speed/value drives

I have this one in a Windows 7 machine, and it's use is transparent and I don't do all those tweaks you read about and I read all about them.

If you want to keep it simple unplug all drives but the DVD, if installing that way, and the SSD drive. Install windows 7. Profit. Than do two things. Make sure disk level indexing is off (which you should be doing anyway) this is under your C: drive properties right under where it says Compress this drive to save space. The indexing shouldn't be set if you installed the way I said, but check anyway. This will not effect windows indexing (which I vote for leaving on even on a SSD drive)

Then update your drives firmware.

Don't worry about cache and indexing, super fetch and all that. Just let Win 7 set all that all up. and all that.

Don't worry about hibernate. Use hibernate if you want, or don't, but you don't need to change it since you are running on a SSD. Same with system restore if you have the room, and you like having it on, leave it on. This drive will automatically over-provision 7% of the drive so you don't need to set that.

Windows will set up your drive just fine. If you want to go research it all and make your own decisions, that's fine I did the same thing. And the above 'simple' installation was what I decided on. (I did 3 separate installations working through various options).. I have tweaks I do, but they are tweaks I do SSD or no SSD.

A lot of information about SSD drives is based on small drives and older controllers. You don't need to worry about how long your drive will last. It will last longer than you will have your computer. Look up the tests on this on the internet to understand how little of an issue this really is. A lot of what is written about SSD's is written by enthusiasts/gamers who are into tweaking systems. If, like me, you like doing this kind of research, great. Otherwise just install windows and use your drive SDD drive like any other drive.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Electronics 840 EVO-Series 120GB 2.5-Inch SATA III Single Unit Version Internal Solid State Drive MZ-7TE120BW

text_fidelity_a:
D-Link Pan & Tilt Wi-Fi Camera (DCS-5009L) (Discontinued by Manufacturer) This camera is yet another product made in China and sold here in the United States for prices equivalent to what we'd pay if the thing was actually made in the USA, which IT IS NOT. The plastic it's made with seems cheap and brittle.

The setup instructions are WRONG and can lead you through a lengthy hell to install and configure the camera. The camera DID NOT HAVE THE MOST CURRENT SOFTWARE and I was forced through an update TWICE because the first one was the wrong one. Yes, the wrong one was recommended on their website. It took a second pass to get the correct version. Speaking of their website, it's a real mess, difficult to navigate, impossible to locate what you need on it, and just plain annoying. Tech support is mostly via email and the one time I did get a human, he didn't know much about anything.

You may want to use the camera's web interface to set up security and so forth. The GOTCHA is the cameras use Java and Java is going to drive your internet security software, firewall and virus protection wild. Java is known to be a welcome mat announcing your computer is open for all manner of malware, virus infections and so on. My security software blocked the install entirely.

Access to the camera remotely is via the D-Link website through an account you set up. To see the camera's video you must go to the website, log in and then view the camera. As video goes from camera to the D-Link website and then to you via your mobile device, the panning and zooming is jerky due to the lag in the up and download of the signal.

If you're looking for a security camera to use while traveling, or out for an evening, this will take care of things--barely. If you want a home security system with multiple cameras, go for a dedicated system with hard-wired cameras, a DVR and a solid wall around it for security. This camera is a toy compared to industrial or home-grade security.
text_fidelity_b: D-Link Pan & Tilt Wi-Fi Camera (DCS-5009L) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
